A persistent higher differential pressure supports restriction; a fluid contamination test addresses a different failure mode, cross-leakage.
example.result: Plan inspection and cleaning using the maker's isolation, plate sequence and tightening instructions. Do not assume every temperature rise requires a new plate pack.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: In a shell-and-tube exchanger, one fluid flows through tubes and the other around them. Baffles guide shell-side flow, but also affect pressure drop. Tube leakage can mix fluids in the direction set by their local pressure difference, which may change when pumps stop.

example.problem: Cooling water contamination appears after shutdown although normal running samples are clean. How could a tube leak explain this?
steps: Compare pressures during running and shutdown; their ordering may reverse.
An isolated pressure or leak test can identify a damaged boundary without assuming the normal running flow direction persists.
example.result: A leak path and a pressure difference together determine contamination direction. Follow an approved test pressure and isolation procedure; excessive test pressure can damage sound tubes.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Fouling adds thermal resistance, but its symptoms overlap with low flow, air binding and changed seawater temperature. Compare an exchanger against a clean baseline at similar duty and flow before deciding that cleaning is the remedy. A single outlet temperature is insufficient evidence.

example.problem: At the same flow and inlet temperatures, a cooler transfers 80 kW instead of its previous 100 kW, and water-side pressure drop has increased.
steps: Estimate heat duty from mass flow, heat capacity and measured temperature change.
The combined thermal and hydraulic changes strengthen the restriction hypothesis; verify instrument accuracy and strainers before opening the exchanger.
example.result: Record performance again after cleaning. Recovery toward the baseline demonstrates the effect of the intervention; lack of recovery directs investigation toward another cause.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Heat exchanger effectiveness compares actual heat transfer with the maximum possible for the inlet temperatures and smaller heat-capacity rate. It differs from thermal efficiency of an engine. The smaller capacity rate sets the maximum because that stream would otherwise cross the opposite inlet temperature.

example.problem: Hot and cold capacity rates are 4 and 2 kW/K. Inlet temperatures are 80°C and 20°C; measured duty is 90 kW.
steps: Maximum duty is Cmin(Th,in − Tc,in) = 2 × 60 = 120 kW.
Effectiveness is 90/120 = 0.75. Cold outlet temperature is 20 + 90/2 = 65°C.
example.result: The effectiveness is 75%, with hot outlet 57.5°C. This temperature pattern requires a compatible flow arrangement; energy balance should agree on both sides within measurement uncertainty.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: An exhaust economizer transfers exhaust heat into water or steam. Soot deposits both resist heat transfer and can become combustible. A declining steam output is therefore a performance clue, while abnormal gas temperatures or fire indications demand the vessel's emergency response rather than routine cleaning.

example.problem: Steam production drops at the same engine load while gas-side pressure drop rises. What should the engineer investigate?
steps: Compare exhaust inlet conditions, feedwater flow and instrumentation with the clean baseline.
Examine approved soot-cleaning history and restrictions without treating a possible soot fire as an ordinary fouling problem.
example.result: Assess cleaning under the maker's procedure and safe operating conditions. Never improvise water application to a hot economizer; distinguish preventive cleaning from the specific fire response.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Waste heat recovery converts part of otherwise rejected energy into useful heating or power. Gross recovered output can overstate the benefit if additional pumps, fans or exhaust backpressure increase fuel use. The useful comparison is the net change at an equivalent ship operating condition.

example.problem: A recovery unit generates 180 kW while its new auxiliaries consume 25 kW. What benefit can be claimed from these figures alone?
steps: Subtract auxiliary consumption: preliminary net electrical output is 155 kW.
Check any added engine fuel consumption or propulsion penalty before converting this into a voyage fuel saving.
example.result: 155 kW is a subsystem result, not yet a complete ship saving. Include availability, low-load performance and whether recovered heat replaces a real demand.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: A steam turbine converts an enthalpy drop into shaft work. Available power depends on steam mass flow, inlet state, exhaust pressure and actual turbine efficiency. Supplying a turbine must not compromise essential steam consumers or boiler water level control.

example.problem: Steam flow is 0.5 kg/s and the ideal available enthalpy drop is 400 kJ/kg. Assume turbine efficiency 70% and neglect generator losses.
steps: Ideal shaft power is 0.5 × 400 = 200 kW.
Actual shaft power is approximately 0.70 × 200 = 140 kW under these assumptions.
example.result: Electrical output will be lower after generator and auxiliary losses. Verify steam quality and operating limits; a calculated power figure does not establish safe turbine admission conditions.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Cogeneration produces useful heat and power from the same fuel input. Its reported total efficiency depends on counting heat that is actually used. Dumping excess hot water overboard does not create an energy-saving credit, even if the recovery equipment is available.

example.problem: A plant consumes 1000 kW of fuel energy, produces 350 kW electricity and supplies 400 kW of useful heating.
steps: Electrical efficiency is 35%; useful combined efficiency is (350 + 400)/1000 = 75%.
If heating demand falls to 100 kW, useful combined efficiency becomes 45%, although electrical output is unchanged.
example.result: Compare operation over the real demand profile. Match recovery capacity to consumers and avoid presenting installed heat-recovery capacity as continuous useful output.

topicTitle: Enerji dönüşüm verimi ve kayıp analizi

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: An energy balance follows energy into useful output, rejected heat and other losses. Successive conversion efficiencies multiply rather than add. Define the system boundary first so that auxiliaries or electrical losses are not counted twice or silently omitted.

example.problem: An engine converts 40% of fuel energy to shaft work and its generator converts 95% of shaft work to electricity. Fuel input is 1000 kW.
steps: Shaft output is 400 kW; generator output is 400 × 0.95 = 380 kW.
Overall conversion efficiency is 0.40 × 0.95 = 38%, before external auxiliaries.
example.result: The remaining 620 kW leaves through heat and other losses. A useful loss analysis assigns each stream to the same boundary and operating condition before selecting an improvement.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Heading describes the bow direction; course over ground describes displacement over the seabed. Leeway can also separate heading from the through-water velocity, so a current triangle that ignores wind is a simplified model. Compare instruments using the same true or magnetic reference and time interval.

example.problem: A vessel makes 10 kn north through the water while a 2 kn current sets east. Assume no leeway. Find the ground track.
steps: Resolve north and east components: 10 kn north and 2 kn east.
The angle east of north is arctan(2/10) = 11.3 degrees; ground speed is sqrt(104) = 10.20 kn.
example.result: Heading 000°T produces COG approximately 011°T. To maintain a northward track, steer into the current and recompute the triangle; do not simply substitute COG for heading.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Speed through water measures motion relative to the surrounding water; speed over ground measures motion relative to the seabed. They are vector magnitudes. Subtracting the two scalar readings gives current speed only when the velocities lie on the same line. A cross-current can increase SOG while also creating an unwanted track offset.

example.problem: The ship maintains 12 kn through water on an eastward heading. Compare a 3 kn following current with a 3 kn current setting north.
steps: With the following current, eastward ground speed is 12 + 3 = 15 kn.
With the cross-current, SOG is sqrt(12² + 3²) = 12.37 kn and COG turns 14.0 degrees north of east.
example.result: The same current speed gives different SOG and track. Use SOG for distance-over-ground estimates, but retain STW and current direction when evaluating propulsion performance or predicting the vessel's path.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Rudder balance describes blade area relative to the stock axis. Area ahead of the stock can reduce actuator torque, but forces still depend on speed, angle and inflow.

example.problem: Two rudders have equal area but different stock positions. Is their required torque equal?
steps: Compare the force's lever arm about each stock.
Include actual blade geometry and operating condition rather than area alone.
example.result: The same force can create different torque. A balanced rudder is not force-free; use the approved steering-gear limits.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Electrical power drives hydraulic flow, which develops rudder torque. Pump operation, pressure and actual movement are separate observations; a running motor does not prove steering response.

example.problem: The helm command changes but rudder feedback does not, although a pump runs.
steps: Compare commanded angle, independent local indication and actual response.
Follow the steering-failure communication and changeover procedure.
example.result: Investigate the control and hydraulic paths. Do not interpret normal motor current as proof that the rudder is under control.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: The telemotor transmits commands; the steering power unit supplies the force. Transmission may be hydraulic or electrical depending on design. Fault isolation separates missing commands from failed execution.

example.problem: Bridge control fails but approved local control moves the rudder.
steps: Check the remote command and feedback paths.
Maintain bridge-to-local communication and use the documented changeover arrangement.
example.result: Local movement narrows the fault but does not clear the complete steering system. Test the restored command chain before normal operation.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: A steering test verifies actual functions, indications, communication and alternatives. A checklist signature or moving display alone cannot establish correct mechanical response.

example.problem: The bridge indicator moves, but nobody verifies local rudder position.
steps: Compare command, bridge feedback and independent local evidence.
Test the required alarms and alternative arrangements using the vessel's approved procedure.
example.result: Record observed performance and defects. A feedback or linkage fault can remain hidden if the test checks only the display.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Backup steering depends on available power, controls and an understood changeover method. Shared components can disable two nominally separate systems, so counting pumps does not prove independence.

example.problem: Both pumps rely on one failed control-power component.
steps: Trace the common dependency and identify the approved alternative control mode.
Establish communication before transferring control.
example.result: Use the vessel's steering emergency procedure. Include common power and control failures in drills and maintenance reviews, rather than testing only individual pump starts.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Fixed pitch describes blade geometry, not constant thrust. Thrust and shaft load depend on rpm, inflow, vessel condition and sea state. Reversal uses the installation's reversing arrangement.

example.problem: Usual shaft rpm produces less ship speed in heavier weather.
steps: Compare draft, environmental conditions and shaft power.
Assess engine loading rather than assuming constant rpm means constant demand.
example.result: The engine may carry more load at the same speed. Use power and operating limits alongside vessel speed when evaluating propulsion performance.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Controllable pitch changes blade angle while the shaft may keep rotating in one direction. Commanded pitch, feedback and actual blade position are distinct; zero indication need not prove zero thrust.

example.problem: Pitch is commanded to zero but thrust remains.
steps: Check feedback and the approved calibration and control arrangement.
Communicate the discrepancy and follow the propulsion-control response.
example.result: Do not rely on the command alone for manoeuvring or personnel safety. Verify actual behavior through the installation's approved test procedure.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Propeller efficiency relates thrust power to shaft power. Cavitation begins when local pressure becomes low enough for vapor cavities to form; collapse can produce noise, vibration and erosion.

example.problem: Vibration increases at one combination of rpm and loading.
steps: Compare operating conditions, hull state and inspection evidence.
Distinguish possible cavitation from imbalance and bearing faults.
example.result: Use the approved response and investigate the cause. Increasing rpm to recover speed can worsen an unfavorable cavitation condition.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Stern-tube seals control fluid exchange while bearings support the shaft. Pressure relationships, including effects of draft, influence leakage direction. An oil-level rise can indicate water entering rather than extra oil.

example.problem: Oil level rises and a sample contains water.
steps: Verify the reading and sample, then compare seal pressures and draft.
Assess bearing lubrication and follow the maker's contamination response.
example.result: Investigate ingress and protect the bearings. Normal oil-supply pressure alone does not establish that the lubricant remains suitable.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Intermediate bearings mainly support radial loads; the thrust bearing transfers axial propeller force into the hull. Monitoring only radial vibration can miss an axial problem.

example.problem: Thrust-bearing temperature rises while intermediate bearings remain stable.
steps: Compare axial load, lubrication and relevant operating changes.
Inspect the thrust load path and its instruments separately.
example.result: Healthy intermediate bearings do not clear the thrust bearing. Apply its specific protection limits and investigate the affected component before unrestricted operation.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: The windlass handles anchor and cable through its wildcat, drive and brake. Environmental loads must be managed through the approved anchoring arrangement; motor torque is not a substitute for a sound brake.

example.problem: The drive continuously holds a heavily loaded cable while brake condition is uncertain.
steps: Assess the operation with the responsible officers.
Verify the designed load-holding arrangement and keep personnel clear.
example.result: Use the approved anchoring procedure and vessel handling to control the situation. Do not improvise a load-holding method around defective equipment.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: A crane's allowable load changes with radius and configuration. Vessel motion, heel and lifting accessories also matter. The least-rated component can govern the lift.

example.problem: A crane rated for 10 t at short radius must lift at greater outreach.
steps: Read the chart at the actual radius and configuration.
Include rigging mass and the vessel's approved operating conditions.
example.result: Do not carry short-radius capacity to full outreach. Confirm the full lift plan, equipment limits and communication before moving the load.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Automatic-tension winches respond to line load but can redistribute forces across the mooring arrangement. Their use must suit the vessel, berth and line plan; automatic mode is not universally preferable.

example.problem: One winch pays out while adjacent lines take greater load.
steps: Assess the operating mode and berth procedure.
Monitor the whole mooring arrangement and exclude personnel from loaded-line danger zones.
example.result: Use the approved mooring plan. Consider how each winch action affects other lines, rather than optimizing one line in isolation.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Weathertight hatch closure depends on seals, compression, drains and securing. A closed-position switch confirms only one part of that boundary; debris or misalignment can still create a leak path.

example.problem: A hatch indicates closed but leaks during an approved test.
steps: Inspect sealing interfaces, drainage and securing points.
Distinguish damaged rubber from inadequate compression or structural misalignment.
example.result: Repair the actual cause and repeat verification. Replacing a seal alone may not correct a closure or alignment defect.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Ramps and lifts contain moving loads and stored hydraulic energy. Hydraulic pressure alone is not a safe support for maintenance beneath a raised structure.

example.problem: An underside inspection is requested while a ramp is raised.
steps: Use its designed mechanical supports and approved isolation procedure.
Verify stored-energy control and exclusion zones before access.
example.result: Never rely solely on a valve or gauge to hold the structure. A hose or valve failure can permit sudden movement even after the pump stops.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Hydraulic pumps supply flow; resistance creates pressure. A variable-displacement pump may reduce delivery at its pressure setting, so high pressure does not necessarily indicate useful actuator work.

example.problem: Pressure reaches its setting but the actuator moves slowly.
steps: Compare delivered flow, command, leakage and load.
Check whether normal destroking or an unintended flow path explains the behavior.
example.result: Pressure and flow answer different diagnostic questions. Do not raise the pressure setting before establishing why the required movement is missing.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Cylinder force depends on pressure and effective piston area. The rod reduces one side's area, so equal pressure produces different extension and retraction forces. Friction reduces ideal values.

example.problem: Piston area is 50 cm², rod area 10 cm² and pressure 100 bar.
steps: Extension force is 10 MPa × 0.005 m² = 50 kN.
Retraction uses 40 cm², giving 40 kN.
example.result: Use the correct working area and load direction. Equal pressure does not mean equal force or equal speed in both directions.

topicTitle: Yön kontrol ve basınç kontrol valfleri

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Directional valves route flow; pressure-control valves regulate or limit pressure. A relief valve is not a positive mechanical lock for a suspended load.

example.problem: A loaded cylinder creeps downward although supply pressure is normal.
steps: Trace load-holding valves and leakage paths.
Secure the load with the approved arrangement before adjustment or disassembly.
example.result: A correct relief setting does not establish safe load holding. Isolate stored energy and verify the intended protective components before maintenance.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Trace a hydraulic circuit from supply through controls and actuators to return, identifying stored energy. Symbols show a defined valve state that may differ from the actual energized state.

example.problem: An actuator moves after its pump is isolated.
steps: Identify accumulators, elevated loads and trapped-pressure sections.
Apply the specified isolation, discharge and verification steps to each energy source.
example.result: Stopping the pump is incomplete isolation. Confirm actual valve states and absence of hazardous stored energy before opening a connection.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Hydraulic cleanliness affects pump clearances and valve motion. Filter efficiency, particle size, water and fluid compatibility all matter; a nominal filter rating alone is insufficient.

example.problem: A servo valve sticks repeatedly after filter replacement.
steps: Check element specification, bypass condition and contamination sources.
Review water, particle, temperature and air-entrainment evidence.
example.result: A new filter cannot correct every fluid problem or prevent continuing contamination. Restore the source conditions and verify the equipment's specified cleanliness target.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Reciprocating and screw compressors use different compression and unloading mechanisms. Motor rotation and discharge pressure do not establish useful delivered flow.

example.problem: A compressor stays unloaded despite rising air demand.
steps: Check the load command, pressure sensing and model-specific unloading mechanism.
Compare actual delivery and receiver pressure trend.
example.result: Use the correct compressor procedure. A running machine can consume power while supplying little useful air, so investigate the full control and delivery path.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Receivers store compressed energy and collect condensate. Relief devices, drains and inspection address different hazards. External paint condition cannot establish internal wall integrity.

example.problem: A receiver repeatedly collects water and lacks recent inspection evidence.
steps: Review drain performance, separator condition and required examination records.
Prepare competent inspection under full isolation and depressurization.
example.result: Never remove fittings under pressure. Correct both retained water and its source; routine draining does not replace a required pressure-vessel examination.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Dryers remove moisture while filters remove specified particles or aerosols. Cooling downstream can condense water even when hot outlet air appears dry, making pressure dew point a useful service measure.

example.problem: Remote pneumatic controls malfunction after air cools in the line.
steps: Check dryer pressure dew point, bypass state and drains.
Investigate oil and particle contamination separately.
example.result: A filter is not a substitute for a dryer. Verify air quality at the required operating condition, including the coldest relevant downstream section.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Starting air turns the engine and must be protected against reverse flow and abnormal combustion entry. Distribution, cylinder valves and protective devices form one system.

example.problem: A starting-air branch becomes unusually hot during engine operation.
steps: Follow the maker's immediate protective response.
Investigate the associated starting valve and protection after safe shutdown and depressurization.
example.result: Do not repeatedly start the engine to reproduce the symptom. Abnormal heating requires prompt, controlled investigation under the approved procedure.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Control-air reliability depends on pressure and cleanliness. Service-air tools can create large demand changes; shared equipment needs an arrangement that preserves essential controls.

example.problem: Several pneumatic tools cause control-air pressure to fall.
steps: Trace shared supply, regulators and priority provisions.
Reduce nonessential demand and restore specified control-air conditions.
example.result: A common compressor does not imply equal consumer priority. Verify that controls retain their required supply during peak service demand and investigate inadequate separation or capacity.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: A generator diesel must respond to changing electrical demand while maintaining suitable speed. Frequency and voltage involve different control functions, so recovery of one does not prove the other is satisfactory.

example.problem: A large motor starts and generator frequency dips sharply.
steps: Compare the load step with reserve capacity and governor response.
Check the approved motor-start sequence and plant load management.
example.result: Assess both prime-mover and electrical behavior. Avoid repeating a heavy load step before understanding an excessive frequency disturbance.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Alternator frequency depends on rotational speed and pole count. Excitation primarily affects voltage and reactive-power behavior; prime-mover input governs real power in a properly controlled parallel plant.

example.problem: A four-pole alternator runs at 1500 rpm.
steps: Calculate f = poles × rpm/120 = 4 × 1500/120 = 50 Hz.
Recognize that changing excitation does not change this speed relationship.
example.result: Diagnose real and reactive load sharing separately. Use the approved synchronization and control procedure rather than adjusting excitation to correct a real-power imbalance.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Emergency generation must remain available after normal supply fails. Independence includes starting energy, fuel and control arrangements as applicable. An unloaded start alone does not prove supply to emergency consumers.

example.problem: The engine starts but its breaker fails to connect the emergency bus.
steps: Check bus condition, permissives and the approved automatic sequence.
Verify actual essential-consumer supply, not only engine running.
example.result: Record the failed connection function and restore it. Readiness concerns the complete power path and the vessel's applicable statutory requirements.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: A composite boiler uses exhaust heat and an oil-fired section. Available exhaust energy changes with engine operation, while steam consumers may continue demanding the same output.

example.problem: Steam pressure falls as the main engine slows and the burner remains off.
steps: Identify the reduced exhaust heat input.
Check steam demand and approved burner mode and permissives.
example.result: A heat-source transition can explain the pressure change. Investigate the control response while preserving water-level and combustion safeguards, rather than immediately assuming a steam leak.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Water treatment controls deposits, corrosion and carryover through different measures. A single chemical dose cannot correct every abnormal result; representative sampling and the specified treatment program matter.

example.problem: Conductivity rises after feedwater conditions change.
steps: Verify the sample and investigate contamination and concentration.
Apply the approved blowdown and treatment guidance.
example.result: Correct the source and repeat testing. Adding chemicals solely to chase one reading can conceal contamination or create a second problem.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Low-water protection, flame safeguards and pressure relief address different boiler hazards. Normal pressure does not establish that heated surfaces remain safely covered by water.

example.problem: Water-level indication becomes unreliable while firing continues.
steps: Follow the approved response to uncertain level and verify independent indications where provided.
Do not bypass the trip or add water blindly to a potentially overheated boiler.
example.result: Establish a safe condition before diagnosis. Evaluate water level, flame and pressure through the specific boiler procedure.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Boiler inspection requires isolation from pressure, heat, fuel, electricity and connected systems. Shutdown is only the beginning of preparation; temperature, atmosphere and access conditions must also be verified.

example.problem: Internal inspection is planned immediately after shutdown.
steps: Confirm depressurization, cooling, isolation and entry requirements.
Arrange competent examination and document deposits, corrosion and damage.
example.result: Use the approved permit and inspection process. Retain measurements and repair evidence so future surveys can assess deterioration rather than only current appearance.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Vacuum lowers seawater's boiling temperature, allowing relatively low-grade heat to drive evaporation. Heating, vacuum generation and condensation interact; output rate and distillate purity remain separate measures.

example.problem: Production falls as vacuum deteriorates at similar heating-water temperature.
steps: Check air ingress, ejector or vacuum equipment and condenser performance.
Compare absolute pressure with the relevant saturation temperature.
example.result: Restore the approved flow and pressure conditions. Increasing heat indiscriminately may mask the fault; verify product quality before accepting the output.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Water quality requirements depend on use. Boiler feed, cooling water and drinking water have different criteria. Low salinity shows little dissolved salt but does not establish microbiological safety.

example.problem: Distillate passes a salinity check. Is that enough for potable service?
steps: Verify the approved treatment, disinfection and monitoring process.
Assess storage and distribution hygiene as well as the generator.
example.result: Salinity is one indicator, not a complete drinking-water assessment. Follow the vessel's potable-water management and testing requirements.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Remineralization and disinfection serve different functions. Effective disinfection depends on delivered dose, contact conditions and monitoring, not simply a running pump.

example.problem: A downstream residual result is below target although the dosing pump operates.
steps: Check reagent condition, actual delivery, water flow, contact time and test method.
Investigate unusual demand or equipment failure before changing settings.
example.result: Restore the approved treatment conditions and verify water quality. Pump motion alone does not establish effective dosing, and excessive dosage is not automatically safer.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Freshwater-generator capacity is rated for stated heat and cooling conditions. Lower production can result from reduced heat input, poor vacuum or fouling; hourly output alone cannot distinguish them.

example.problem: Output falls after the main engine load decreases.
steps: Compare heating-water flow and temperatures with rated conditions.
Check vacuum and condenser behavior before ordering cleaning.
example.result: Normalize the comparison before judging deterioration. Reduced available heat can explain lower output without a new fault; product-quality monitoring remains necessary at every production rate.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Centrifugal separation depends on density difference, droplet size, viscosity and residence time. Excessive throughput or unsuitable temperature can reduce removal even at normal bowl speed.

example.problem: Outlet water contamination rises after feed rate is increased.
steps: Compare throughput and temperature with the unit's approved range.
Check bowl and water-discharge performance.
example.result: Return to a verified operating condition and investigate outlet quality. Continuous running does not prove that the separator is achieving the required separation efficiency.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: A purifier separates two liquid phases and solids in its intended arrangement; a clarifier primarily removes solids. Modern phase-control designs vary, so internal configuration must follow the specific machine.

example.problem: A clarification setup receives oil containing substantial free water.
steps: Check whether the configuration can remove that water safely.
Use the approved mode and internal arrangement for the actual feed.
example.result: Do not assume equivalent water removal from the two labels. Monitor outlet quality after configuration changes and use the maker's instructions.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: In machines using a gravity disc, its selection helps position the oil-water interface. Fuel density at operating conditions, temperature and throughput influence the correct choice; other designs use different controls.

example.problem: A purifier loses its water seal after a fuel change.
steps: Confirm density and temperature against the maker's selection guidance.
Check assembly and throughput before replacing the disc.
example.result: An incorrect interface can impair separation or lose oil through the water outlet. Use the unit-specific chart and verify the corrected condition.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Automatic desludging relies on operating water, timing and mechanical bowl response. A commanded discharge does not prove solids were released or the bowl resealed correctly.

example.problem: The discharge command appears normal but expected discharge evidence is absent.
steps: Check operating-water supply and sequence indications.
Investigate bowl operation after the required isolation and shutdown.
example.result: Do not repeatedly force cycles without diagnosis. Verify both sludge removal and resealing before returning the separator to continuous service.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Heating lowers viscosity and supports separation, but appropriate temperature depends on the fuel and equipment. Settling, separation and filtration perform different functions and cannot automatically substitute for one another.

example.problem: A new fuel uses the previous batch's temperature setting.
steps: Compare its properties with the approved separation range.
Check actual temperature, throughput and outlet quality together.
example.result: Set treatment for the actual fuel. A universal temperature or a clean downstream filter does not prove that every separable contaminant has been removed.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Purification can remove certain water and solids, but cannot restore every depleted additive or reverse chemical degradation. Appearance, viscosity and chemical condition answer different questions.

example.problem: Water content improves after purification but viscosity remains abnormal.
steps: Compare the complete oil analysis with supplier and maker limits.
Investigate contamination or degradation sources and assess renewal needs.
example.result: Do not declare oil restored solely because water fell. Treatment has limits; continuing degradation requires correction at its source and verification of lubricant suitability.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Multistage compression with intercooling can reduce work and discharge temperature. Unequal stage behavior may indicate valve, cooling or pressure-distribution problems.

example.problem: First-stage discharge temperature becomes unusually high.
steps: Compare interstage pressure, cooler performance and valve condition with the baseline.
Check whether pressure ratios remain appropriate for the design.
example.result: Investigate the interacting stages instead of adjusting only the final pressure switch. Protect the compressor according to its specific temperature and pressure limits.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Intercoolers cool air between stages; aftercoolers cool final delivery. Cooling condenses moisture, which must then be separated and drained. Good heat removal alone does not establish dry air.

example.problem: Aftercooler air is cool but the receiver collects excessive water.
steps: Inspect separator and drain performance.
Compare air flow and ambient moisture when evaluating condensate quantity.
example.result: Cooling can increase collected liquid. Verify its removal; otherwise the system may deliver water to receivers and controls despite a satisfactory outlet temperature.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Automatic drains must remove condensate without continuous air loss. A stuck-closed drain permits carryover; a stuck-open drain wastes air and can lower pressure.

example.problem: The compressor cycles frequently and a drain continuously passes air.
steps: Check the drain's commanded and actual state using its approved test.
Investigate contamination or valve damage preventing closure.
example.result: Repair and verify normal operation. Permanently shutting the drain's isolation valve merely exchanges air loss for an unresolved moisture-removal problem.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Compressor valve leakage can reduce capacity and increase temperature. Deposits, damage and incorrect assembly may produce similar symptoms, so performance trends guide inspection but do not identify one cause conclusively.

example.problem: Receiver filling takes longer and one stage runs hotter.
steps: Compare stage pressures, temperatures and approved capacity-test results.
Inspect valves and cooling after isolation and depressurization.
example.result: Verify repair with a controlled performance comparison. Longer filling time establishes reduced delivery, not automatically a defective valve.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Receiver inspection addresses pressure integrity, corrosion and protective fittings under the applicable statutory and class regime. Draining and external checks support care but do not replace required competent examination.

example.problem: An externally sound receiver repeatedly retains water and has an overdue inspection.
steps: Review records and arrange the required examination.
Prepare full isolation, depressurization and safe access.
example.result: Paint condition cannot prove internal integrity. Correct the drainage problem and retain examination evidence for future condition comparisons.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Residual-fuel behavior depends on viscosity, density, stability and contaminants. Heating supports handling but does not remove every harmful component. Two acceptable batches are not necessarily compatible when mixed.

example.problem: Filters block after two residual fuels are mixed.
steps: Review compatibility evidence and mixing history.
Check for precipitated material while protecting the fuel supply.
example.result: Individual specification compliance does not prove mixture compatibility. Segregation and suitable testing can prevent a problem that heating alone may not resolve.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: A fuel specification applies to an identified grade and edition. Compliance does not guarantee compatibility with another batch or suitability for every engine and treatment plant.

example.problem: The supplier cites ISO 8217 without a grade or edition.
steps: Obtain the exact contracted specification and test evidence.
Compare it with maker-approved fuels and treatment capability.
example.result: The standard's name alone is incomplete. Do not substitute assumed limits for the actual grade, edition and contractual requirements.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Fuel viscosity generally falls with increasing temperature, but the curve differs among fuels. Reference-temperature viscosity does not directly establish engine-inlet viscosity.

example.problem: Two nominally similar fuels require different heater temperatures for the same injection viscosity.
steps: Compare their actual viscosity-temperature characteristics.
Verify the viscometer and engine-inlet conditions.
example.result: Control the required fuel condition rather than copying a temperature setting. Excessive heating can cause other handling and leakage problems, particularly with low-viscosity fuels.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Cloud point concerns wax appearance; pour point concerns low-temperature flow under its test conditions. Filters may block before the fuel ceases to pour.

example.problem: Fuel still pours but cold filters block.
steps: Check cold-flow information and actual fuel temperature.
Investigate wax formation and use approved heating and handling guidance.
example.result: Pour point alone does not establish filterability. Include the coldest relevant pipes and components when planning temperature control.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Water and sediment can overload treatment and harm injection equipment. Sample location and timing affect representativeness; a clear upper sample may miss bottom contamination.

example.problem: A top sample looks clean while tank drains release water and sludge.
steps: Compare representative samples with drain evidence.
Investigate ingress, settling and treatment performance.
example.result: Do not use appearance at one location to clear an entire tank. Follow the approved sampling and draining method and verify correction of the contamination source.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Settling provides residence time for some water and solids to separate; service storage supplies treated fuel. Actual routing determines whether fuel received the intended treatment.

example.problem: The service tank fills while the separator is bypassed.
steps: Trace the valve route and identify possible untreated fuel entry.
Protect engine supply and follow the approved contamination response.
example.result: Tank names do not guarantee content quality. Verify fuel condition and restore the correct process route before normal use.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: A viscosity controller adjusts heating according to its measurement. Sensor error or poor circulation can make a stable displayed target misleading.

example.problem: The controller shows target viscosity but an independent check suggests fuel is too thin.
steps: Verify calibration, sample conditions and heater-valve response.
Compare actual inlet temperature and viscosity.
example.result: Investigate the discrepancy before changing the target. A functioning feedback loop can regulate accurately around an inaccurate measurement and still supply unsuitable fuel.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Purification removes separable contaminants under appropriate flow, temperature and bowl conditions. Continuous running does not guarantee removal of fine abrasive particles.

example.problem: Outlet analysis shows poor contaminant removal.
steps: Check throughput, temperature, configuration and sludge-discharge performance.
Verify that inlet and outlet samples are comparable.
example.result: Correct the treatment condition and repeat quality checks. Running hours alone do not demonstrate that the separator is protecting the engine.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Automatic filters backflush retained particles. Frequent cycles may indicate contamination, unsuitable viscosity or element problems; a bypass can preserve flow while exposing downstream machinery.

example.problem: Backflushing suddenly becomes frequent after bunkering.
steps: Compare differential pressure, fuel condition and separator performance.
Check the maker's permitted response and element condition.
example.result: Investigate the warning rather than lengthening the interval to hide it. Restore filtration and avoid an unapproved continuous bypass.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Homogenization disperses material into smaller particles or droplets; it does not remove every contaminant. Its role must be assessed within the approved treatment system.

example.problem: A homogenizer is proposed instead of separation.
steps: Compare what each process removes or merely disperses.
Check engine requirements and maker-approved treatment arrangements.
example.result: Uniform appearance is not proof of purification. Smaller dispersed contaminants may remain in the fuel and continue downstream.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Changeover involves compatibility, temperature, viscosity and the retained volume of the complete system. Switching tanks does not instantly replace fuel in heaters, filters, returns and injectors.

example.problem: Low-sulphur fuel is selected just before entering a regulated area.
steps: Use the approved changeover calculation and procedure.
Monitor inlet conditions and record verified completion.
example.result: The selector position alone does not prove compliant fuel has reached each consumer. Plan sufficient time for the actual system and operating demand.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Bunker mass estimation requires compatible volume and density reference conditions. Soundings also need the vessel's trim and list corrections; meters and tank calculations should be reconciled.

example.problem: Corrected volume is 100 m³ and density at the same reference condition is 0.96 t/m³.
steps: Check temperature corrections before multiplying observed hot volume by reference density.
example.result: Retain calibration, readings and assumptions. A numerical agreement without matching reference conditions can conceal a quantity error.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: The BDN documents a delivery but does not replace quantity checks or representative samples. Compare its identity and declared properties with the order and actual fuel.

example.problem: The BDN grade differs from the purchase specification.
steps: Check delivery records and sample identity with the responsible parties.
Document the discrepancy through the approved process.
example.result: Do not silently alter the record or assume equivalence. Preserve traceability while suitability and contractual questions are resolved.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Sulphur compliance concerns the fuel actually used in the applicable area, or an approved equivalent arrangement. Carrying compliant fuel does not prove every consumer receives it.

example.problem: One auxiliary remains connected to a higher-sulphur service system before ECA entry.
steps: Trace each relevant consumer's actual supply.
Complete and verify the approved changeover or equivalent arrangement.
example.result: Check applicable area and date requirements and retain the required records. Inventory alone is insufficient evidence of operational compliance.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: A representative sample needs an appropriate sampling method, identity, seal and chain of custody. Laboratory accuracy cannot compensate for an untraceable bottle.

example.problem: A disputed delivery has an unsealed sample with no recorded point or time.
steps: Identify the limitations of that sample.
Preserve properly identified retained samples and follow the agreed dispute process.
example.result: Do not treat the untraceable result as conclusive evidence of the delivery. Representativeness and sample identity are part of the technical evidence.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Bunker disputes require factual, contemporaneous records. Measurement assumptions and sample identity matter; protecting machinery should remain separate from assigning responsibility.

example.problem: Ship and supplier quantity figures differ by 3 t.
steps: Reconcile temperature, density, remaining quantities, tank corrections and meter records.
Record the discrepancy and notify responsible parties through the approved process.
example.result: A difference warrants investigation, not an automatic accusation. Preserve evidence while managing any suspected unsuitable fuel safely.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Refrigeration compressors move vapor and raise its pressure. Liquid entering a compressor can damage components; oil return and suction conditions therefore matter alongside discharge pressure.

example.problem: A compressor becomes noisy after a sudden load change.
steps: Check approved suction, superheat and oil indications.
Investigate possible liquid return without repeatedly restarting a distressed machine.
example.result: Do not diagnose solely by sound. Protect the compressor and use its specific operating limits and investigation procedure.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: The evaporator absorbs heat while refrigerant evaporates; the condenser rejects absorbed heat plus compressor work. Poor condenser heat rejection can raise discharge pressure even when the evaporator load is unchanged.

example.problem: Condensing pressure rises after seawater flow falls.
steps: Check seawater supply, strainers and condenser condition.
Compare heat-rejection conditions before changing the refrigerant charge.
example.result: A high-pressure symptom does not automatically mean overcharge. Restore verified cooling conditions and evaluate the whole cycle.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: An expansion valve controls refrigerant admission; a thermostatic or electronic valve uses feedback according to its design. Incorrect sensing can cause starvation or liquid return even when the valve itself moves.

example.problem: Superheat fluctuates after a sensing bulb is relocated.
steps: Check mounting, thermal contact and insulation against the maker's instructions.
Compare actual suction conditions with the control signal.
example.result: Do not adjust the valve to compensate for incorrect sensing. Restore the installation and verify stable operation at representative loads.

topicTitle: CFC, HCFC ve HFC soğutucu gazlar

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Refrigerant families differ in environmental impact, pressure behavior and material compatibility. A similar name or cooling capacity does not establish that one is a drop-in replacement.

example.problem: A refrigerant substitute is proposed for an older system.
steps: Check approved refrigerant, lubricant, seals, pressure ratings and control settings.
Confirm legal handling and technician requirements.
example.result: Use an engineered, authorized conversion where appropriate. Do not mix refrigerants or infer compatibility solely from a supplier's performance claim.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: CO₂ and ammonia have different hazards despite being termed natural refrigerants. CO₂ systems can involve high pressures; ammonia presents toxicity and compatibility concerns. System design and emergency response must match the substance.

example.problem: Two refrigerant cylinders carry different natural refrigerants. Can the same charging arrangement be used?
steps: Verify substance identity, rated equipment and approved connections.
Check the relevant safety data and system procedure.
example.result: The natural label does not mean interchangeable or harmless. Use refrigerant-specific equipment, training and emergency arrangements.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: ODP describes ozone-depletion potential; GWP compares climate impact over a specified time horizon. These indicators address different environmental effects and do not describe toxicity or pressure hazards.

example.problem: A refrigerant has zero ODP but substantial GWP.
steps: Separate ozone and climate effects.
Assess leakage, energy use, safety and applicable restrictions in addition to either index.
example.result: Zero ozone-depletion potential is not a complete environmental or safety assessment. Compare alternatives using the relevant full set of criteria.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Ozone-depleting substances and HFC phasedown obligations involve different instruments and schedules. Applicable restrictions depend on substance, jurisdiction and date; environmental policy is not a universal replacement procedure.

example.problem: An existing system needs refrigerant during maintenance.
steps: Identify the exact substance and applicable current handling and supply rules.
Check approved recovery and service arrangements before obtaining a substitute.
example.result: Do not infer a global blanket ban or retrofit deadline from a protocol name. Confirm the actual requirement and equipment compatibility.

topicTitle: Soğutucu akışkan şarj ve geri kazanım

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Charging and recovery require known refrigerant identity, suitable cylinders and measured quantities. Pressure alone is not a reliable charge indicator across changing loads and temperatures.

example.problem: A technician proposes adding refrigerant until suction pressure looks normal.
steps: Check for leaks and establish the maker's charging method.
Use specified measurements and recovery equipment, preserving refrigerant identity.
example.result: Do not mask a flow or heat-transfer fault by adding charge. Record recovered and added quantities and verify operation after the actual fault is corrected.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: A cold room's air temperature and product temperature respond at different rates. Door opening, loading, defrost and airflow affect performance. One sensor near the evaporator may not represent the stored provisions.

example.problem: Air temperature recovers quickly after loading, but products remain warm.
steps: Check product loading, airflow and representative temperature measurements.
Review defrost and door conditions without obstructing circulation.
example.result: Air recovery alone does not establish safe product storage. Apply the vessel's food-storage limits and monitoring procedure to the actual goods.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: A reefer controls its cargo environment according to the commodity and instructions. Supply-air and return-air readings mean different things, and ventilation settings can be as important as temperature.

example.problem: A reefer shows correct supply temperature but abnormal return temperature.
steps: Compare cargo instructions, airflow and loading arrangement.
Check alarm history and probe function before changing the setpoint.
example.result: A correct setpoint is not proof of correct cargo condition. Follow the carrier's reefer procedure and escalate unexplained deviations.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Central cooling separates seawater heat rejection from freshwater distribution. A header temperature can remain acceptable while one branch receives inadequate flow. Pump and valve behavior must be assessed across both sides.

example.problem: One consumer overheats while the central cooler outlet remains normal.
steps: Check branch flow, valve position and local restrictions.
Compare the affected consumer's inlet and outlet conditions.
example.result: A healthy common cooler does not prove adequate local circulation. Investigate the branch before changing the whole plant's temperature setting.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Different machinery circuits may require different temperature levels and flow. High- and low-temperature systems must be traced according to the actual installation rather than treated as interchangeable cooling supplies.

example.problem: A cooler works but cylinder-jacket temperature remains abnormal.
steps: Identify the relevant circuit, thermostat or mixing valve and consumer flow.
Check whether the fault lies in heat rejection or temperature regulation.
example.result: Changing seawater flow may not correct a freshwater-control problem. Use the documented circuit and engine-specific operating limits.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Alarms identify abnormal measurements; protective trips limit consequences. Sensor accuracy, setpoint suitability and actual process condition are separate questions. Repeated reset does not remove the cause.

example.problem: A refrigeration high-pressure trip recurs after reset.
steps: Check condenser cooling and verified pressure indications.
Follow the maker's restart criteria and investigate the initiating fault.
example.result: Do not defeat the protection to maintain cooling. Restore a verified safe operating condition before restarting and record the recurring fault.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Air conditioning combines heat removal, moisture control, filtration and air distribution. A cold coil does not ensure that occupied spaces receive adequate conditioned air or ventilation.

example.problem: The cooling coil is cold but a cabin remains warm.
steps: Check fan operation, filters, dampers and duct flow.
Compare supply and room conditions before increasing refrigeration output.
example.result: Trace heat and air paths separately. A distribution fault can leave a room uncomfortable while the refrigeration cycle operates normally.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: An AHU's filters, coils, fans and dampers work together. Filter loading raises resistance and may reduce flow; bypassing filters can contaminate coils and ducts rather than solve the maintenance issue.

example.problem: Supply airflow falls as filter differential pressure rises.
steps: Compare the reading with the specified service criterion.
Inspect and replace or clean the approved element as required.
example.result: Verify restored flow afterward. Do not permanently bypass the filter or infer adequate ventilation merely from fan operation.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Cooling coils remove sensible heat and may condense moisture; heating coils add heat. Fouling reduces performance and condensate drainage affects hygiene and water carryover.

example.problem: Water appears downstream of a cooling coil.
steps: Inspect drain pan, trap and drainage condition.
Check airflow and coil cleanliness against the approved arrangement.
example.result: Treat drainage and air velocity as part of the diagnosis. Lowering the temperature setting alone can increase condensation and worsen the symptom.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Relative humidity depends on temperature as well as water-vapor content. Cooling without moisture removal can raise relative humidity; cooling below dew point can remove water through condensation.

example.problem: Air is sensibly cooled while its moisture content stays unchanged.
steps: Recognize that saturation capacity falls as temperature falls.
Relative humidity rises until condensation conditions are reached.
example.result: Do not equate cooler air with drier air. Use humidity, temperature and dew-point evidence when evaluating dehumidification performance.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Duct design balances air delivery against pressure loss and noise. Restrictions and poorly balanced branches can starve distant spaces even when total fan flow seems adequate.

example.problem: A nearby cabin has strong airflow while a distant cabin has little.
steps: Check branch resistance, dampers and filter condition.
Measure or verify distribution before increasing fan speed.
example.result: Higher speed can increase noise and power without correcting an imbalance. Restore the intended distribution using the approved balancing procedure.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Fresh air supports ventilation while exhaust removes contaminated or moisture-laden air. Recirculation can control temperature without providing enough outside air. Intake location and pressure relationships affect contamination movement.

example.problem: A space stays cool but odors and moisture persist.
steps: Check actual outside-air and exhaust flow, not just recirculation.
Verify dampers, intake condition and the designed pressure relationship.
example.result: Thermal comfort is not proof of adequate ventilation. Restore the approved air exchange and investigate contamination sources.
